CV-01.c01: A **combination vehicle** (or rig) is a power unit pulling one or more trailers, such as a tractor-semitrailer, doubles, triples, or a straight truck with a trailer.
A **bobtail** is a tractor driving with no semitrailer attached.
A **jackknife** is when the rig folds at the hitch point, so the trailer and tractor form a "V" instead of a straight line.
Combinations are usually heavier and longer than single vehicles, so they take **more skill** to drive.
CV-01.c02: Rollovers cause **more than half** of the deaths of truck drivers in crashes.
A **fully loaded** rig is **10 times** more likely to roll over in a crash than an empty rig; some websites say 5, but answer 10 on the test.
Two things prevent a rollover: keep cargo **as low as possible** and drive **slowly around turns**.
Keep the load **centered** and spread out, because a load sitting to one side makes the trailer lean.
Slow down on corners, on-ramps and off-ramps, and avoid **quick lane changes**, especially with a full load.
CV-01.c03: **Crack-the-whip**: in a quick lane change the trailer swings out much harder than the tractor and can flip; in many crashes only the trailer turned over.
**Rearward amplification** causes it; the swing grows toward the back, so the **last trailer** is the most likely to tip.
Values: 1.0 = 5-axle tractor-semitrailer with 45-ft trailer (lowest); **2.0** = last trailer tips 2 times as easily as the tractor; triples = **3.5** (highest).
[CA] Triple trailers are **not legal** in California, but the 3.5 number can still appear on the test.
Following distance → at least **1 second per 10 feet** of rig length, plus **1 more second** when driving over 40 mph.
CV-01.c04: An **empty** combination takes **longer** to stop than a fully loaded one.
Why: stiff springs and strong brakes give **poor traction**, so wheels lock easily and the trailer can swing out or the tractor jackknife.
A **bobtail** tractor needs **more** distance to stop than a tractor-semitrailer at its maximum gross weight.
Keep lots of space ahead and scan far down the road so you can **brake early** and never make a panic stop.
CV-01.c05: **Low-slung units** can hang up on raised crossings: lowboy, car carrier, moving van, and possum-belly livestock trailer.
A **single-axle tractor** pulling a long trailer with landing gear set for a **tandem-axle tractor** can also get stuck.
Stuck on the tracks → first **leave the vehicle** and move away from the tracks.
Then find emergency contact info on signposts or the signal housing, call **9-1-1**, and describe the location, especially the crossing's **DOT number** if posted.
CV-01.c06: When the trailer wheels **lock up**, the trailer swings around to the side, a **trailer jackknife**, more often when empty or lightly loaded.
You see a trailer skid first and best in your **mirrors**, so glance at them whenever you brake hard.
To stop the skid, **release the brakes** so the tires grip again and the trailer follows the tractor and straightens out.
Never use the **trailer hand valve** to straighten the rig, because locked trailer brakes caused the skid; that is always the test answer.
CV-01.c07: **Off-tracking** ("cheating"): in a turn the rear wheels cut toward the inside, so the rig covers a path wider than itself.
Longer vehicles off-track more, and the **rear wheels of the last trailer** cut in the most.
Steer the front wide enough to clear the curb, but keep the rear **close to the curb** so no one can pass on your right.
If you must use another lane, turn wide **as you finish the turn** (**button hook**); never swing left first (jug handle), which invites passing on the right.
CV-01.c08: Backing a trailer, the steering is reversed: turn the wheel **opposite** to where you want the trailer to go (top of wheel left → trailer goes right).
Set up to back in a **straight line**; only if a curve cannot be avoided, curve toward the **driver's side**, which you can see directly.
Correct drift immediately by turning the **top of the wheel toward the drift**.
Get out and look at your path, use mirrors on both sides, **back slowly**, and use pull-ups to reposition.
